title: LN4 Fusion announces intention to enter FIA Formula 2 Championship in 2027
excerpt:
LN4 Fusion has confirmed its intention to enter the team application process with a view to entry in the FIA Formula 2 Championship in 2027.

The team is co-founded by 2025 Formula 1 World Champion Lando Norris and today confirmed that it acquired selected assets of AIX Racing. It will also undertake application procedures to join the F2 grid next season.

LN4 Fusion also confirmed that Rene Rosin will serve as Team Principal, with Guillaume Capietto serving as Racing Director for the team’s wider operation.

Norris detailed the plans currently in the works along with a driver development programme, having come through FIA Formula 2 himself en route to F1 and winning the World Championship last year.

Co-founder Norris said: “I’ve been really lucky to have some amazing people around me throughout my career, and I know that getting to Formula 1 takes so much more than just talent. You need the right people around you, the right support and the right opportunities at the right time.

“That’s what these two projects are all about. LN4 Fusion is about building a race team that can compete with the best in junior motorsport, with great people and a great environment for drivers to develop. The LN4 Legacy Programme is about helping talented young drivers get opportunities they might not otherwise have.

“For me, they naturally fit together. I want to help create opportunities for the next generation, both on and off the track, and hopefully make a real difference to young drivers coming through the sport.”

FIA Formula 2 CEO Bruno Michel commented: “I’m very pleased to see that Lando Norris, who is the first F2 graduate to have become a Formula 1 World Champion, is showing interest in getting involved in an F2 team. LN4 Fusion has taken over AIX Racing and will be applying for an entry for the next three-year cycle of Formula 2, which will run from 2027 until 2029.”

Team Principal Rosin added: "Motorsport has always been my passion and my professional life. I am thrilled to have the opportunity to contribute my experience to an independent, vision-driven sporting programme with strong backing, a clear long-term vision and the resources required to build it properly. Having Lando on board adds a further dimension to this project. He has come through the junior single-seater ranks and understands its demands. His involvement will make a real difference to the team.

"We want to develop a pathway through junior single-seaters and create an environment in which drivers, engineers and sporting personnel can perform at the highest level. My role is to focus on racing: building and managing the sporting programme, creating the right technical environment and helping the team become competitive."

title: WHAT TO WATCH FOR: The key storylines post summer break in Monza
excerpt:
The summer break is over which means it is time to return to racing, as the paddock heads to Monza for Round 10 of the 2026 season.

The Temple of Speed is a favourite for many drivers, teams and fans, and with the title fight closer than ever we can expect another fascinating trip to Italy.

But before we hit the track, here are a few storylines to look out for this weekend…

THE TITLE CHASING TRIO

Heading into the weekend, Nikola Tsolov leads the Drivers’ Standings on 167 points with Gabriele Minì and Rafael Câmara just 20 and 22 points behind respectively.

Monza has previously played an integral role in the title fight, such as in 2024 when Gabriel Bortoleto’s championship comeback started with an iconic victory from last in the Feature Race.

Tsolov, Minì and Câmara would rather not tempt fate by starting at the back this weekend, but a strong three days on F2’s return to action could prove vital in the championship battle.

Tsolov and Câmara are strong contenders for the title going into Monza

There are not many rounds left in the season so each point will be vital, and with all three drivers having achieved multiple victories they will be confident of being back on the top step in Monza.

The results this weekend will not decide the title for either of this three, but it could give them the momentum boost they need going into the final part of the season.

READ MORE

How to watch Round 10 in Monza: TV, Session times and more

FORMULA 2’s 10TH SEASON: Lando Norris on how F2 prepared him for Formula 1

A PUNCHER’S CHANCE

For a long time Alexander Dunne had been firmly in the title fight, but he returns to the paddock 59 points behind Tsolov.

The Rodin Motorsport driver still had a chance having had had a consistent year, but he has not been on the podium since Barcelona.

Last time out in Budapest, damage in Qualifying left him down starting down the order in both races, and he did not score a single point.

But Dunne has shown what he is capable of doing in a Formula 2 car and as previously said we have seen title comebacks start in Monza.

Dunne and Beganovic both have an outside chance of claiming the title

The Irish driver will not be the only driver hoping to start their fightback however, as the likes of Noel León, Kush Maini and Dino Beganovic will also be keen to close that gap.

The top three may be far ahead but a lot can happen in Formula 2, and will there is still being a chance for many drivers, they will be battling hard in Monza.

DO YOU WANT POLE?

On Formula 2’s previous nine visits to Monza, only twice has the pole-sitter converted that starting position into Feature Race victory.

The first was Oscar Piastri in 2021 and the second was Luke Browning last season.

We have seen Bortoleto win from last, we have also watched Tadasuke Makino take victory from P14, and Mick Schumacher from seventh.

This is to say that the results in Qualifying should not be how the drivers define success this weekend. Piastri and Browning proved you can win from pole, while others showed that you can make a fightback through the field.

Bortoleto won from the 2024 Monza Feature Race from the back of the grid

So even if you’re favourite driver does not take pole on Friday, they are still very much in the running for victory in both races around Monza.

HOME TEAMS EYEING SUCCESS

The drivers will be eyeing victory no doubt, but so will the teams, especially two Italian outfits in the field – TRIDENT and PREMA Racing.

The latter have an incredible record at Monza, having taken seven victories there in Formula 2. This includes a famous double in 2023 when Frederik Vesti won the Sprint and Oliver Bearman claimed Feature Race victory.

READ MORE

Nikola Tsolov completes first F1 test with Racing Bulls

Spielberg victory ‘best day of my life’ after tough couple of seasons says Bennett

TRIDENT on the other hand have not been able to replicate that success but they do have two podiums at the Temple of Speed – Bent Viscaal finished second in 2021 and Richard Verschoor in 2024.

They have shown great pace this year with Laurens van Hoepen and John Bennett, so they will feel they are very much primed for their first win in Monza.

As for PREMA, it has not been the smoothest of years, but there is no better place to get back on track than at home.

title: FORMULA 2’s 10TH SEASON: Lando Norris on how F2 prepared him for Formula 1
excerpt:
In 2025 Lando Norris became the first FIA Formula 2 alumni to become Formula 1 world champion, and recently we caught up with him to reflect on it all.

From his favourite moments in the championship to what he learned, the current McLaren driver also shared his advice for next generation of F2 drivers looking to join him at the next level.

HOW DID F2 PREPARE YOU FOR YOUR MOVE UP TO F1?

“You learn something new in every category. In F2, I raced against incredible drivers—some of whom I’m racing today in F1. Most drivers come from Formula 2, so you’re already competing against some of the best in the world, including future world champions and race winners. That level of pedigree forces you to perform at a high level.

“You also visit many of the same racetracks that Formula 1 uses, which is very important. F2 provides good track time through races and qualifying, giving you opportunities to learn how to drive under pressure, race, and handle different scenarios. For almost every situation you encounter in Formula 1, you’ve already learned how to deal with it in F2, and that’s crucial.”

Norris picked out his win in Bahrain as one of the highlights of his season in F2

WHAT’S YOUR ADVICE FOR THE NEXT GENERATION OF F2 DRIVERS LOOKING TO MAKE IT TO F1?

“Don’t try to do anything overly excessive just to impress people. For some, it might take one year; for others, it might take three. There’s no point rushing or thinking you need to know everything immediately. Don’t feel you have to impress on a big scale in front of F1 teams. Instead, focus on maximising what you can do yourself and learn as much as possible.”

READ MORE

Nikola Tsolov completes first F1 test with Racing Bulls

Spielberg victory ‘best day of my life’ after tough couple of seasons says Bennett

WHAT WAS YOUR FAVOURITE WIN, MOMENT OR OVERTAKE?

“There were a lot of incredible moments in F2. I had fun battles with George at Monza. Starting the season the way we did in Bahrain was pretty good. I also enjoyed many races at Monza and Abu Dhabi. There were a lot of moments I enjoyed racing against George and Alex, among others.”

DO YOU HAVE A FAVOURITE MEMORY FROM OFF THE TRACK?

“Off track, I was with Carlin. I did another year with Carlin and worked with many people I’d known for years. We enjoyed a lot of moments together. I learned a great deal about engineering—how to set up a car and analyse data—which is always important.”

HOW SPECIAL IS IT TO BE THE FIRST FORMULA 1 WORLD CHAMPION FROM FORMULA 2, CONSIDERING THE FIELD IS LARGELY F2 ALUMNI?

“It’s very special to look back and hear about these things. You don’t think about it at the time, but having your name written down somewhere for a good reason is something to be proud of. I’m happy I was the first, and the first of what will be many.”

title: Nikola Tsolov completes first F1 test with Racing Bulls
excerpt:
Nikola Tsolov has completed his first laps in a Formula 1 car, taking part in a Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) opportunity with Racing Bulls around Imola.

The Bulgarian driver was at the wheel of the VCARB02 on Thursday, racking up 690Km over the course of the day.

Reflecting on his opportunity, the Red Bull Junior Team driver said that he was hugely thankful to the team and thrilled with the opportunity.

"First TPC day in a Formula 1 car done, and I’m super happy with how today went. I really enjoyed every lap and it’s difficult to put into words what it means to finally get this opportunity.

“A massive thank you to VCARB and the Red Bull Junior Team for believing in me and giving me this opportunity.

“It’s something I’ve been working towards my whole life, so to finally experience it is pretty incredible. I still don’t think I’ve fully comprehended what we achieved today, but I enjoyed every lap and hopefully I’ll get the chance to add some more kilometers soon.”

Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane added: "Today was a really positive step for Nikola. He adapted quickly to the car and showed the composure you want to see from a driver taking on an F1 car for the first time.

“The outing is part of the ongoing development plan the team runs for its junior drivers, giving them the tools, the mileage, and the environment to develop. We've seen time and again what this pathway can produce, and it’s days like today that are part of how we keep building it."

Tsolov leads the FIA Formula 2 Drivers’ Championship by 20 points heading into Round 10 at Monza next weekend.

title: Noel León on enjoying racing in 2026, eyeing a place in Formula 1 and the title fight
excerpt:
It has been a season of incredible ups and a few downs for Noel León, but most importantly it is a campaign he is thoroughly enjoying.

The Campos Racing driver has impressed in 2026, achieving three victories, including at the Budapest Feature Race before the summer break.

That leaves León fifth in the Driver’s Championship with 94 points – the third highest placed rookie in the Standings.

“It's been a very good first half of the season,” says León. “I was dealing with a lot of ups and downs, but very good ups. But in general, I'm pretty happy with my rookie season.

“The positive is that I've been able to show how strong I am, doing pole positions, wins, fastest laps in races. The pace that I've been having with the team has been amazing.

“The bad ones are that we have not always been able to maximise Sundays, especially at the Red Bull Ring. I started P1 and finished P7, so that was a hard one for me to lose.”

León achieved his first Feature Race win prior to the summer break in Budapest

POSITIVES AFTER A DIFFICULT 2025

A day after León’s victory in the Monte Carlo Sprint Race, his Team Principal Adrián Campos said: “It's good that Noel won yesterday, but to be honest, he shouldn't have won because he should have been starting further in the front today. He deserved to be fighting for pole on Friday.”

That quote was put to the Mexican driver and although he acknowledged that he could have had better qualifying results he pointed to a few factors, like traffic and Red Flags, that have affected the outcomes.

But given the difficulties of León’s 2025 FIA Formula 3 campaign – where he finished 17th in the Standings with 36 points – he takes plenty of positives from the fact that he is fighting at the front.

READ MORE

Ragebaiting, iRacing and being closely matched: Getting To Know Teammates Alexander Dunne and Martinius Stenshorne

Laurens van Hoepen on bouncing back in 2026, TRIDENT’s improvements and competition in F2

“It's a big change to be honest,” says León reflecting on the difference between last year and this season. “Last year many people including myself felt I was in the position where I was going to fight for the championship and then at the end I was struggling to get points.

“So it was a very difficult one. Mentally, I was not prepared for that after making a big jump to a championship-winning team for my second year. I felt I was going to win every race.”

“But it was not even possible to think about that after just the first race. I then got a very nice opportunity with Campos, so I am very thankful for them, with all my sponsors as well for the help to get this chance.”

The Mexican driver revealed where he believes the big difference has been between him and Tsolov this season

COMPARING HIMSELF TO TSOLOV

That experience of battling in the midfield last year is what León believes has been a major difference between him and Tsolov.

His Bulgarian teammate currently leads the Drivers’ Standings and has achieved six victories of his own. But León feels that their pace is quite similar and that the difference comes in how they are able to extract their best on race days when fighting at the front.

“I think compared to Nikola, where I was mainly missing at the beginning of the season was that at the front you race different,” he explains. “At the front you need to think different, you need to do different things.

“I was not used to it because I was used to be fighting for P15, P20. So it's very difficult, because it’s very different. So I think at the beginning of the season, that was the main thing, that he was able to extract performance better.

“The pace was very similar, but just in terms of how to extract it, he was able to do it better. It was difficult. It's good to have a teammate like this, that is doing good, so you know where to learn and where to go forward.”

León knew how critical his Budapest weekend was before the summer break

CONTINUING AN ENJOYABLE YEAR AND MAKING A NAME FOR HIMSELF

León felt that the double header in Spa-Francorchamps and Budapest before the summer break was critical to his season.

Speaking after his win in Budapest he said: "As I said before the weekend, this was going to be the weekend that we turn around things and we keep moving forward."

The Campos driver now wants to continue that form after the summer break. Not only his title charge on the line but with him also having desires on making a name for himself in Formula 1.

READ MORE

10 Years of Friendships: Getting To Know Rivals Dino Beganovic and Gabriele Minì

Formula 2 in 2021: Oscar Piastri sets new standard with familiar names in the fray

“There’s still a long season ahead,” he says. “I think everybody felt like the season was going to end in two weeks before the summer break, but there's still a long season ahead.

“Obviously, I want to be on the map for everyone in the Formula 1 paddock. But to be on the map for everyone you cannot wait until the last race. You need to already be in their thoughts and already on the radar.

The Campos driver is keen to continue what has been an enjoyable season

“I want to be there. I know what I need to do to be on the radar. That's why I'm pushing myself and pushing the team to be there. I'm very confident with the team and this is also giving me confidence to be on the radar for Formula 1.”

In addition to that, the Mexican is enjoying his time with the team and wants that to continue when F2 goes to Monza next weekend.

“Obviously, when we are not fighting for the podium or for P1, it's not as enjoyable,” he says. “But it's been a very good season, to be honest, to be back on the fight for a championship, to be there in the top five, not far from top three.

“At the beginning of the season we had great pace, so obviously Campos is helping a lot and I'm in a very good position with them.

“The team is also in a very good position, so everything is very nice, very enjoyable. I'm having a good time, to be honest,”

title: Ragebaiting, iRacing and being closely matched: Getting To Know Teammates Alexander Dunne and Martinius Stenshorne
excerpt:
Teammates Alexander Dunne and Martinius Stenshorne are a close pair, not only on the track but away from it as well, and recently we caught up with them to talk about their friendship.

The Rodin Motorsport duo revealed how they used to annoy one another, how they work together to get better, who won their arm wrestle competition and much more.

HOW LONG HAVE YOU KNOWN EACH OTHER?

Martinius Stenshorne: Since 2019 maybe?

Alexander Dunne: 2020? We’ve known each other since 2017, that’s when we first race against each other. But friends, I would say 2020.

WHAT WERE YOUR FIRST IMPRESSIONS OF THE OTHER?

Dunne: I don’t really remember. Mainly a lot of the stuff we did together originally was on the sim. We have quite a big friend group who all play with each other on iRacing and numerous different games. So it started back then when we were still in karting.

Stenshorne: I don't even remember it was so long ago. I think you were always screaming at me and I was ragebaiting Alex. Alex was very easy to rage bait back then.

Dunne: Martinius is the type of person that whenever we're playing, it's a bit better now, but when we were younger, he was always the type of person where he would just annoy everyone. Everyone thought it was funny, but he was the type of person that would just annoy everyone. He's just liked to rage bait and say stupid stuff. It was always funny.

Stenshorne: Alex was very easy to rage bait so it helped. It's not so much like that anymore.

Dunne: He was always winding people up and I would always give in so we would end up screaming at each other.

Both drivers recalled their first impressions of each other and their arguments over the simulator

The duo revealed what they think the other would do if they were not a racing driver

WHO KNOWS THE MOST ABOUT CARS?

Dunne: Probably Martinius to be honest.

Stenshorne: Karts, I win! Cars? I don’t know.

Dunne: I don't think we're the type of people that care that much.

Stenshorne: I don't care. I don't care about cars at all. I drive a big van

Dunne: He’s a crafter.

Stenshorne: I have a big van with my go-karts in the back, so I think that shows that I don't really care about cars.

Dunne: I like cars and I like the idea of having a nice car, but knowing the inside, I don't really care about it too much.

Stenshorne: I would just like to have a car that sounds good.

WHO’S ON THEIR PHONE THE MOST?

Dunne: Probably me.

Stenshorne: Alex!

BUT WHO TAKES THE LONGEST TO REPLY?

Stenshorne: Maybe me.

Dunne: You’re not that bad.

Stenshorne: Maybe, but he's for sure more on his phone than me. I think my screen time is just three hours or something.

Dunne: I would say on average, it's probably seven and above. But it's been a lot higher than that, quite a few times.

Stenshorne: I think if we take the screen time on the sim, it's worse.

The duo also spend a lot of time training together at Rodin

SO WHO’S ON THE SIM THE MOST AND WHO IS IN THE GYM THE MOST?

Stenshorne: Sim, probably Alex. Gym, I don't know to be honest, and running, maybe me more.

Dunne: Neither of us spend that much time on our sim.

Stenshorne: Yeah, we do spend time on the sim, but not much driving.

Dunne: Exactly. We spend a lot of time in our sims doing different stuff, but actually driving on the sim, at least on our home sims, we don't do half as much as what we used to do and in the sim at Rodin, it's pretty similar. Whenever we go for a run or train at Rodin, we always do it together, so it's pretty similar.

READ MORE

Formula 2 in 2021: Oscar Piastri sets new standard with familiar names in the fray

Roman Bilinski: ‘Points a sign of progress’ as improvements continue

WHAT’S THE BIGGEST THING YOU HAVE LEARNED FROM EACH OTHER?

Dunne: I think in general for me in comparison to last season and now, I think Martinius and I have been very similar in pace every weekend. So for me to have another aspect of learning and someone to push against me, I think for me is quite important. Out of all the teammates I've had so far, he's probably the one that I felt like I've been the closest with. So to have someone to push you on is a good thing.

Stenshorne: Yeah, it's always like that. So then it's good to have so you can compare and see. Because you're never driving every corner perfect, so then it's always nice to have a reference when both are quite fast and we can compare.

WHO WOULD WIN IN AN ARM WRESTLE?

Stenshorne: We’ve done that. I won.

Dunne: Martinius is quite strong.

Stenshorne: We need to do it again, but not in front of everyone.

title: Laurens van Hoepen on bouncing back in 2026, TRIDENT’s improvements and competition in F2
excerpt:
Laurens van Hoepen and TRIDENT separately had tough 2025 campaigns, but they are bouncing back together in 2026.

The Dutch driver joined the team for the final three rounds of last season, coming off the back of a tough year in FIA Formula 3 – where he finished 12th in the Standings.

They did not score any points in those last few races, but after an extensive amount of work at both post and pre-season testing they started the 2026 campaign in style.

Van Hoepen finished third in the Melbourne Feature Race and second in the Miami Sprint and also took pole position at Round 3 in Montreal.

Results have been mixed since then, but the 20-year-old returned to the podium in the Budapest Sprint, and heads into the summer break eighth in the Drivers’ Standings.

“It's been going well,” starts van Hoepen. “I think there's a lot of positives like the speed we've had so far has been really good.

Van Hoepen's season got off to a good start with a podium in the Melbourne Feature Race

“Of course there's also been some missed opportunities and I think we could have been a lot higher in the standings if we had a bit more luck and did things a bit differently. But at least the positives are that we're very quick.”

THE FIRST PODIUM AND SIGNING WITH TRIDENT

After scoring just two points last season, the signs were there that TRIDENT were going to be competitive, with their performance at the Barcelona pre-season test catching the eye.

When times were at there fastest on the final day’s morning session, van Hoepen was fourth on the leaderboard.

READ MORE

10 Years of Friendships: Getting To Know Rivals Dino Beganovic and Gabriele Minì

Formula 2 in 2021: Oscar Piastri sets new standard with familiar names in the fray

So that first podium in Melbourne confirmed what the Dutchman and his team had known going into Round 1, which was they had improved a lot over the winter and were now in the fight.

“It meant a lot because it showed that the hard work that we had done over the winter and that we were still doing was paying off,” he says.

“Obviously TRIDENT had a very difficult season, but the reward of a podium for all their hard work was super nice. It also gave us extra motivation to keep working in this way and to keep going.

Van Hoepen is enjoying his time working with TRIDENT as they both bounce back from difficult 2025 campaigns

That podium was also a confirmation of what van Hoepen had known when he signed for the team last year – which was that the potential to fight at the front was there.

“The way they made me feel, the way they were thinking about certain things just made it very attractive to sign for TRIDENT,” he recalls.

“Of course they had a bad season, but I also had a bad season, and there was definitely a lot of potential there. The way they were ready to work and help me was something that maybe some other teams didn't really show as much.

“That's why I think it was really good that we chose for TRIDENT, and now it's paying off. We've been working hard, we're able to extract potential from the car. I think it's definitely going in the right direction.”

REBUILDING HIS OWN CONFIDENCE

Not only did TRIDENT need those opening few rounds to confirm their hard work but after a trying year, van Hoepen would have wanted a good start just as much as them.

After a strong rookie F3 campaign in 2024, the Dutch driver returned in 2025 with the hopes of fighting for the title, but it never quite happened for him.

Van Hoepen is feeling confident in the car now after his difficulties in 2025

Van Hoepen ended up on the podium twice – finishing third in both the Monte Carlo and Monza Sprint Races – and he admits this created a lot of self-doubt.

“It was difficult because at some point you do start to lose confidence,” he explains. “Even though at the beginning you're like, ‘okay, it's a bad round’, but if the bad results keep happening at some point you start to doubt yourself as well, which is then difficult.

READ MORE

Roman Bilinski: ‘Points a sign of progress’ as improvements continue

Alexander Dunne: ‘Speed is there but results will come’ as he targets return to winning ways

“I think as a driver, you should always have confidence in yourself. But then at some point, when it's not going your way, you start to doubt yourself, which then is really not what you want.”

So where are his confidence levels now?

“Now I feel very good,” he replies. “I have a lot of confidence in myself and in the team. I'm happy where I am. I think the people around me are super, which also gives me a lot of confidence in myself and me being able to do the job that I need to do.”

The Dutch driver has also talked about his aims for the rest of the season

AIMS FOR THE REST OF THE SEASON

While this season has been positive, Van Hoepen also conceded that there had been a few missed opportunities for him and the team.

When talking about the goals for the rest of the season, he says: “The main focus is to do the best we can. I think fighting for a top five every round should be the target.”

But the TRIDENT driver acknowledges that the level of competition within the championship means he and the team have their work cut out for them to achieve this.

“I mean, since I was like 10 years old, we always wanted to compete against the best,” he says. “Then to do that in F2 is of course very nice.

“I think it's the only way to improve, to be able to fight against the best because otherwise, if you win everything, you don't learn. So I think it's very, very good.”

title: 10 Years of Friendships: Getting To Know Rivals Dino Beganovic and Gabriele Minì
excerpt:
Dino Beganovic and Gabriele Minì recently figured out that they have known each other for 10 years and that got them reminiscing about their time together.

From their stint as teammates to their on-track battles, the current Formula 2 rivals reflected on the best and worst parts of the last decade, as well as their first impressions and what they learned from each other.

HOW LONG HAVE YOU KNOWN EACH OTHER?

Gabriele Minì: Since 2016, 10 years.

HAPPY ANNIVERSARY! HOW WILL YOU CELEBRATE?

Dino Beganovic: It means a lot. We have had some great battles on track this year as well, so we will celebrate like that.

Minì: We are going to give a slipstream to each other out of each corner to celebrate.

Beganovic and Minì have known each other for 10 years and first met in karting

WHAT WAS THE FIRST IMPRESSION OF THE OTHER?

Minì: The first serious time we met was probably in F4.

Beganovic: That was properly when we started to know each other. But for me, my first impression of him was in 2016, my first couple years in Italian karting, and before that he was dominating everything, so I was obviously looking at him. Then after we started racing quite a lot in 2017, 2018, 2019 in karting, but we never really spoke. But 2020 we were teammates and we had good times.

Minì: I remember the first time we met quite well. Of course we were always fighting in karting. He was always starting at the front. Always! Every time in every final, he was on the front row. Every time! Then the first time we started to speak was more in 2020, and he was really really quick, especially in the first test we did, he was super quick.

WHAT WAS IT LIKE BEING TEAMMATES?

Beganovic: It was nice. We pushed each other so hard because we knew each other, so we pushed each other even harder. So it was quite nice.

READ MORE

Formula 2 in 2021: Oscar Piastri sets new standard with familiar names in the fray

Roman Bilinski: ‘Points a sign of progress’ as improvements continue

WHAT DO YOU SAY WERE EACH OTHER’S BEST QUALITIES?

Beganovic: I would say that with Gabriele is that when we're off the track, at least when we were teammates, we were able to separate our lives from racing which was quite nice. On the track he's always been fast, in my opinion.

Minì: We always fight so hard. I mean we have also had some crashes, but that's part of it. As you saw even in Miami, we can fight really hard without one or the other getting pushed off or going into the wall, which is not common every time.

The duo talked about the ability to race wheel-to-wheel with one another

WHAT WAS THE WORST CRASH?

Minì: Race 2 in Dubai.

Beganovic: Ah yeah that was really bad.

Minì: It was already really tense after Race 1 because we fought really, really hard. He was a lot quicker, but I was trying to hold on for dear life, and I got the wrong message. I thought it was the last lap, so I almost put him in the wall.

I didn't realise it was that close, and then in the end I let him by because I thought the race was over. I just said yes, I started celebrating and then they told me good job, good job, and then we started pushing again. Then in Race 2, we were starting close again and we crashed.

Beganovic: Yeah, that was bad. We didn't crash in Race 1, we crashed in Race 2.

Minì: But it was so useless that crash. There was no point in doing it. We were out of the points, it was a reverse grid race, we were in P15 or something, so there was no point in that crash. No point! It was so stupid!

WHAT’S THE BIGGEST THING YOU’VE LEARNED FROM THE OTHER?

Beganovic: I think in F4 when we started as teammates, it's a bit more technical but Gabriele was really good at keeping the car very stable with his pedals. It’s something that I learned quite a lot from him.

Minì: For me it was his race pace, especially in F3, he was always really, really fast. Once again, it's a bit more on the technical side but it's the type of information that you get from every teammate you race with, and this is something I keep with me.

Both drivers reflected on their time as teammates including with Arvid Lindblad in Formula 3

WHAT WAS YOUR FAVOURITE THING TO DO AS TEAMMATES?

Beganovic: That was to go eat sushi.

Minì: We were always going. We had some adventures that we did even with Arvid that were really funny.

Beganovic: Also in F4 we were always going to go eat sushi. Always! We were eating so much we could barely go home. We were sharing an apartment because I lived close to PREMA and when he was coming he stayed in the apartment.

Minì: From the apartment it was like a 20-minute walk, but on the way back home it was 40 minutes.

READ MORE

Alexander Dunne: ‘Speed is there but results will come’ as he targets return to winning ways

Inspired by his father with a tribute to a legend: Colton Herta on his 2026 Helmet Design

HOW COOL HAS IT BEEN TO SHARE THE LAST 10 YEARS OF THIS JOURNEY WITH EACH OTHER?

Beganovic: It is nice. Also he is featured in my documentary because we have quite similar backgrounds. None of us really come from a very rich family and so in that sense it's even more special. We have raced many of these guys for a long time but it makes it a bit more special that we kind of have similarities in that way.

Minì: Yeah, exactly. It’s very much the same to be honest.

title: Formula 2 in 2021: Oscar Piastri sets new standard with familiar names in the fray
excerpt:
We continue to celebrate 10 years of FIA Formula 2 and look back to the 2021 campaign as Oscar Piastri and PREMA Racing secured an impressive double

Our look back at the FIA Formula 2 Championship and road to 10 years of racing continues with the 2021 campaign.

Oscar Piastri became the first driver to win the FIA Formula 3 and FIA Formula 2 titles in consecutive seasons as a rookie, setting a new standard that future Champions would aim for.

Several future F1 drivers made their names known, and records were broken in what was a competitive season of F2 racing.

Here’s a look back at some of the top moments.

THÉO POURCHAIRE BECOMES YOUNGEST F2 WINNER

Pourchaire secured his first F2 victory at 17 years old to become the youngest winner in Championship history at the time

Though his record would eventually be beaten by Arvid Lindblad in 2025, Théo Pourchaire announced himself on the F2 stage in Round 2 and around the streets of Monte Carlo.

The Frenchman became the Championship’s youngest pole sitter in Qualifying, before going on to take top honours around the Principality in the Feature Race for ART Grand Prix.

Having earned his first Pole Position in the Championship, Pourchaire would not be denied. He controlled the start to retain his advantage into Turn 1 and kept his foes comfortably at bay.

READ MORE

Roman Bilinski: ‘Points a sign of progress’ as improvements continue

Alexander Dunne: ‘Speed is there but results will come’ as he targets return to winning ways

At 17 years, nine months and two days of age, the French driver stated his intentions as one of the big names in the Championship to keep an eye on in the coming years.

It was the first of his two race victories in 2021, as he later went on to take P1 in the first Monza Sprint Race en route to fifth in the Drivers’ Championship.

PIASTRI STARTS HIS MARCH TO THE TITLE

Piastri started an unstoppable streak in Monza of poles and Feature Race wins

The eventual Champion took an early season Sprint Race victory in Round 1, earning top spot in the second Sprint of the weekend.

However, it wasn’t until Monza and Round 5 that the Australian earned his first F2 Feature Race victory, and it set the tone for the remainder of his campaign.

It was a second consecutive pole for the PREMA Racing driver, and he’d keep an exclusive hold on top spot in Qualifying through to the end of the season.

His evident pace through the early phase of 2021 was on full display around the Temple of Speed, as he retained the lead in the first part of the race. He relinquished the lead to Dan Ticktum after an early Safety Car but eventually regaining top spot with a subsequent Safety Car intervention.

An early stoppage due to a Red Flag after a crash involving David Beckmann and Bent Viscaal brought the Feature Race to an early close, but it was Piastri’s weekend and a sign of things to come.

FOUR IN A ROW

The Australian won the title in the final round to go back-to-back across F3 and F2

Having battled with Zhou Guanyu and PREMA teammate Robert Shwartzman for the majority of the season, Piastri’s form in the final leg of the campaign was undeniable.

The Australian carried on his form from Monza, converting pole position into Feature Race victory at each subsequent event. The streak remains the F2 record for consecutive Feature wins today.

New to the F2 calendar for 2021 was Jeddah, and Piastri doubled up that weekend, mastering the fast and flowing nature of the street circuit to take Sprint Race two and the Feature Race top step along with it.

Piastri clinched the title in the final round at Yas Marina, with a P3 finish in the first Sprint Race enough to move him out of reach in the points standings.

10 Years of Formula 2

FORMULA 2’s 10th season: Lando Norris on F2 preparation en route to World Championship in Formula 1

Formula 2's 10th Season: Oliver Bearman on his favourite win and most memorable moments

Bruno Michel on 10 years of Formula 2, F1 Champions and the future

A fourth consecutive and final Feature Race win of the season was the perfect ending to his impressive campaign, and by the end he had only been off the Sunday podium once all season, missing out on a top three in the season-opening round in Sakhir.

His title was his third-consecutive crown in the junior formulas, and second in the official FIA Pyramid after taking top honours in FIA F3 in 2020.

Only Gabriel Bortoleto has gone on to follow in his footsteps so far in winning the F3 and F2 titles in consecutive seasons as a rookie.

It laid down the blueprint and set the bar for what young drivers hopeful of making it to F1 aim to achieve in the championships.

Next Up

title: Roman Bilinski: ‘Points a sign of progress’ as improvements continue
excerpt:
It has been a mixed rookie campaign for Roman Bilinski, but the DAMS Lucas Oil driver believes a positive European phase of the year can help things.

The Polish driver secured points in eight of the 12 races from Monte Carlo through to Budapest, including a P2 finish in the Principality.

Bilinski says that despite his P17 ranking in the Drivers’ Standings, the 2026 season has been more positive than the points situation suggests.

“I'll say the European phase, actually, all things considered has been relatively positive because we had five races in a row in the points, which is something to look at and be proud of,” he explained.

“Of course, I would have preferred to have a big points finish to really boost you up in the championship, but to consistently show we can fight in that range for five to six races in a row is something very positive.”

Alongside Bilinski at DAMS this season has been Dino Beganovic. The Swede has been instrumental in the Pole getting up to speed.

He says the Scuderia Ferrari Driver Academy talent has been a useful reference to compare himself against, and his methodology has impacted his own approach to the F2 weekends.

Bilinski says the team has made great improvements over the course of 2026 and more strong results will come

“Dino is an experienced driver. He's driven the Ferrari Formula 1 car quite a few times as well. So to learn from someone like that is fantastic and interesting ways, seeing new things, everything, how he feeds back, how he reports is just all very important stuff for me to learn from and to then try and show that I can do as well.

“I'd say the biggest thing has been getting right on it in Practice and Qualifying sessions, and I think it's really shown in the last few rounds. FPs have been very strong for me. Qualifying has been getting a lot stronger as well.

“So this is all something very positive for myself. So now it's just trying to get those big points, finishes to boost us up in the championship, and I truly do believe we can do it, especially with how we've shown our performance can be in the last few rounds. We think we can get that and we deserve to get that.

READ MORE

Alexander Dunne: ‘Speed is there but results will come’ as he targets return to winning ways

Inspired by his father with a tribute to a legend: Colton Herta on his 2026 Helmet Design

“A lot of things haven't gone our way, but a lot has been out of our hands, but that’s part of our sport. So I’m looking forward to the next rounds trying to bounce back.”

With the European leg of the campaign coming to a close on the other side of the summer break, the DAMS driver says they have learned a great deal over the busy period.

Consistent point-scoring results have coincided with improvements both from an operational and driving perspective, with Bilinski eager to add more to his tally in Monza and Madrid.

The DAMS driver is aiming to surge up the Championship order in the coming rounds

He says that the recent results have added conviction to the direction the team is heading in, and they will be targeting a rise up the order in the Championship before the end of the year.

“I think in terms of the driving and within the team, we've really understood what needed to be done, and that is starting to show. 100% we're going in the right direction and I think lots of people can see that.

“I'd love to be racing every day. But for sure, the summer break is good but it's very important to come back from that and be stronger than where we left off from.

“It's going to be all about training, understanding and then applying what we’ve learned to the next rounds. So not so many holidays, but I love what I do and so it's okay for me.

“I hope to keep the form that we've got going at the moment, because it's been strong. But I hope those big race results start to come in and show what we can do, and begin to reflect that in the standings because we deserve it.

“For myself, the team, it's been difficult and now it's time to prove to everyone what we can do.”

title: Alexander Dunne: ‘Speed is there but results will come’ as he targets return to winning ways
excerpt:
Currently fourth in the Drivers’ Championship, Alexander Dunne has put together a season of great consistency but one that’s missing a victory so far.

The Rodin Motorsport driver has been on the podium five times this year so far, has a further four top five finishes and shown incredible speed in Qualifying.

In fact, up until Budapest, Dunne hadn’t failed to finish inside the top four on a Friday all year. Overall, Dunne says he’s been satisfied with his efforts, even if results haven’t gone his way.

“In general, it's been not too bad. I think we've been relatively consistent. I think qualifying has been a major strong point, being in the top three every weekend since Miami, which of course is really nice.

“Being consistent in quali is really important. I think that's definitely something I'm happy about. Then in terms of races, I think pace we need to improve a little bit, but we're getting there.”

The Alpine Academy driver is competing in his second FIA Formula 2 campaign, and he believes his experience from last year is counting for a lot this time around.

However, combined with natural one-lap pace, he says he is more confident across the board and working well with the same Rodin team he debuted with in 2025.

“I think it's a bit of both. I learned a lot from quali last year, there was also a few areas as a rookie I needed to improve on, which I think I've done a good job focusing on this year.

Dunne says one-lap pace is strong but race pace is a focus ahead of the next part of the F2 season

“The team also do a very good job with the car as well. The car is always in the window of where we want it to be, which, of course, makes it a lot easier as a driver.

The first phase of the season has brought podiums but no wins. Dunne says that the missing ingredient is race pace, but that lessons have been learned which formed the basis for strong results regardless.

He says that has come with experience, confidence within his team and self-belief that he can turn tricky situations around, without chasing for the impossible.

Dunne added that he’s sure things will come good in the final phase of the campaign after the summer break is over.

READ MORE

Inspired by his father with a tribute to a legend: Colton Herta on his 2026 Helmet Design

Instinct versus input: How I Race with Mari Boya

“Whether we have the pace to win or the pace to finish fifth, whatever it is, I think we just always need to try and finish as high as we possibly can.

“If the start of a race hasn't gone to plan or if something happens in the middle, I think you just need to reset and maximise on what's possible on the day.

“That's what we've tried to focus on to make sure we get the most points out of every weekend. Race pace is probably the main area of focus, let's say. The last few rounds we've made a step forward and I think Spa was definitely a step in the right direction.

“So I'm pretty confident that we'll be challenging and back to normal pace for wins and things like that pretty soon. Definitely a couple of things that we found that seem to be working consistently. If what we've figured out is true, then I think we should be back to normal.”

The Alpine junior driver says he's focused on himself and maximising results wherever possible

Looking ahead to Monza and when racing resumes, Dunne has no major targets or goals outside of maximising results.

His wait for a win has gone on longer than he’d have liked, but the Irishman is confident he can make it happen before the end of the year, whether that’s in Monza, Madrid or beyond.

Beyond that, he’s not looking at the Championship table, and will instead aim to keep himself out of trouble in the upcoming races which he says will be exciting rounds.

“I just want to try and maximise myself every weekend and get the most out of what we've got. And where we end up is where we end up. I'm not really too focused on that at the moment to be honest.

“Monza's always an enjoyable one, a track I like and it's always fairly exciting, qualifying and a bit of chaos as well, which is always good for the fans. And then Madrid, I'm really looking forward to it.

“From what I've seen, the track looks pretty cool. It looks very high speed and it's a street circuit as well. So I think the fact that it's also going to be a new track for the whole group will make it very exciting.”

title: Inspired by his father with a tribute to a legend: Colton Herta on his 2026 Helmet Design
excerpt:
Colton Herta is hard to miss out on track, with his striking helmet one that has caught the eye of many fans around the world and those in the paddock.

Recently, we caught up with the Hitech driver to talk about the design and the inspiration, and he revealed all…

TRIBUTE TO A MOTORSPORT LEGEND

“So my helmet design, it was pretty easy because it's very similar to my fathers. So that's kind of what the basis is.

“There are little updates to it to modernise it a little bit from when he was driving in the '90s, but still I think if you look at it side-by-side, the main kind of features are still there. Something that kind of stands out to me or something I've done is the 98 with The Union Jack.

“The 98 with the Union Jack on the back is basically to pay respects and in remembrance for Dan Wheldon in the best way that I like to remember him, which is winning the Indy 500 in 2011, driving the 98.

Herta is paying tribute to Dan Wheldon at the back of his helmet

“So that's why. I have no ties to the UK, but that's why I run a Union Jack on my helmet.

“I would say him and Dario Franchitti were two of my favourites. Tony Kanaan was up there also, I really liked him. But those were guys that were teammates with my dad when I was growing up.

READ MORE

Formula 2's 10th Season: Oliver Bearman on his favourite win and most memorable moments

Martinius Stenshorne on the 2026 season, life with Rodin, rebuilding confidence and F1 hopes

“A lot of people called it the super team because there was him, Dario, Tony, and Dan. So obviously they had a lot of impact on my life growing up and going to the racetrack. So I was always drawn to cheering for them, especially Dan.

“It was also super cool when he came back and won the Indy 500 for my dad's team in 2011, his last win. So it was super, super cool, and now it's exciting to watch Susie, his wife, and her boys race in Europe and in the US.

“So it's a cool thing, and I feel very very honoured to be able to run it.

The American driver also spoke about how the colours have changed over the years

BUILDING ON THE ORIGINAL DESIGN

“I have no clue why this was my dad’s design to be honest. I think the colours are super close to representing like the US flag, obviously with the red, white, and blue. But initially, the colours weren't like this, they were a little bit lighter.

“I changed the trim often on my helmet, so it's not always white. So it's not to mimic the American flag, but that's just how it's worked out. I think some of the stuff like the stars represent it.

“I've always been a fan of honeycomb, but it’s kind of gotten outdated, the honeycomb stuff, so I don't really do it anymore, but you can see a little bit on the back.

“But it's a great design. I've had to add some stuff like the front label here to get Cadillac on there as well. It is a little more hectic. I do like a simpler design, but I think it looks really good.”

A SPECIAL HELMET?

“I did a special helmet for Nashville in 2024, the season finale. I ended up winning that race actually, but it was a complete colour change.

Herta revealed what he would do to match the Cadillac livery

“I think it matched the race car, so it was black, yellow, grey, and white. A much darker helmet, and I think that looked great.

READ MORE

Gabriele Minì on title fight, life at MP Motorsport, dealing with pressure and conversations with Alpine

Dino Beganovic on the 2026 season, learning from Hamilton and Leclerc and gaining confidence with Ferrari

“I would love to do something like that. Obviously, if I drive for Cadillac one day I'll have to do something similar to match the car at some races, but then for the main thing I'm not really a guy that likes to change his helmet design all the time and run special helmets a lot.

“So maybe just a few, but for the most part, I like my design and I kind of like the heritage behind it.”

title: Instinct versus input: How I Race with Mari Boya
excerpt:
PREMA Racing driver Mari Boya has embarked on his rookie campaign in FIA Formula 2 in 2026.

With plenty of racing mileage now under his belt, we asked the Spaniard how his style has changed over the years, what the big challenges of F2 are and how he likes to balance his setup.

“I would say I'm an aggressive driver, especially on braking. I would point to that as something you have as an instinct. Looking at data, I would say I am never missing time on an entry of a corner. Maybe at some point it's too much and exit is not there, but it's a bit of a compromise.

“To be honest, style, I don't think it's changed that much. Maybe at the start, you don’t have more knowledge about things and your instinct is changing on its own, just because of having more knowledge, but the style itself doesn't change that much.

Boya stepped up to F2 this season with PREMA Racing

“We are coming from karting where, already at that point you’re set in your ways more or less, but the instinct of pushing that much and being on the limit is always there. But over time, you end up having more knowledge with the car.

“When setting up the car, it’s something that depends on the car you’re driving, so as a driver you must be able to adapt to the direction that is quickest, not always what you like.

READ MORE

Formula 2's 10th Season: Oliver Bearman on his favourite win and most memorable moments

“I will always go for a stable rear on the entry, as I'm a driver that pushes a lot the entry, it's most likely that I'm suffering some instability on the entry, but when I have this I'm able to be super quick.

“For me, it’s the ideal thing, being able to push the entry and then having the front mid-corner when the entry is done.

The Spaniard is focused on getting back into the points following his score in Spa

“Differences between F3 and F2 - it's weight difference. For me it's the biggest thing. Then the procedures, but it's still a racing car. You just maybe need to be a bit more patient with it, as it's heavier in the weight transitions and everything like that.

“The F3 is a car much more light, aggressive, nervous, and in F2 maybe you have to be a bit smoother on some transitions because you need to wait a bit more the weight transition. But for the rest it's not that big a difference.”

title: Martinius Stenshorne on the 2026 season, life with Rodin, rebuilding confidence and F1 hopes
excerpt:
Martinius Stenshorne has had a mixed season but he is determined to end it on a high after the summer break.

The Rodin Motorsport driver made a fast start to the campaign, qualifying in the top four in each of the four rounds – even converting P3 in Montreal into a maiden victory.

But since finishing fifth in the Monte Carlo Feature Race, Stenshorne’s results have dipped – he scored no points in Barcelona, Spielberg and Silverstone.

However the Norwegian bounced back with a podium at Spa-Francorchamps, finishing second in the Sprint Race.

With more positive results, Stenshorne is ninth in the Drivers’ Standings with 59 points, and speaking before the break, he reflected on his rookie campaign.

“Recently, it’s not been very good, I must say,” says Stenshorne. “We did three rounds without scoring any points. We were a bit disappointed with that after having such a good start to the season, scoring very often and when we didn't it was because of crashes.

Stenshorne achieved his maiden victory at the Montreal Feature Race

“I think we can be extremely happy with the first four rounds, then from round five to seven I think, it was not very good. But I think we know now what was wrong, so I think we can be still happy with what we've done.

“We did some big changes for Spa and it helped. I think I had a bit of margin there and the races again were good.”

READ MORE

Formula 2's 10th Season: Oliver Bearman on his favourite win and most memorable moments

Gabriele Minì on title fight, life at MP Motorsport, dealing with pressure and conversations with Alpine

NEW LIFE AND REBUILT CONFIDENCE AT RODIN

Stenshorne and Rodin is a new partnership for 2026, and so far, he is enjoying the experience.

From nicknames to the atmosphere within the group and the performance of the car, the 20-year-old is happy to be a part of the team, which includes good friend Alexander Dunne.

“I have enjoyed it so far,” he says. “Obviously, me and Alex, we've known each other for a long time. So we were already very good friends before I joined Rodin.

“But the team in general is really chill. Everybody's quite relaxed, and of course, the car is fast as well. So far, it's been great. Obviously, it helps when things are going well as well.”

Stenshorne is enjoying his time working at Rodin Motorsport this season

This season with Rodin has also helped Stenshorne contend at the front more consistently after a tough two years in Formula 3.

The Norwegian finished 13th in his rookie campaign and fifth in his second, scoring three victories across both seasons.

But Stenshorne felt he never consistently showed his best self in F3, and he is glad to be able to do so this year.

“Obviously, we got the first win in Canada, the first podium as well,” he continues. “I think it's been possible for a very long time especially this year.

“I always thought I was capable of doing these things. But to finally show it with the speed we've had so far this year feels good. Obviously in F3, we were there sometimes, there or thereabouts, but never fully at the front.

“You get a bit frustrated because you know that you can be there. Seeing people you fought with before doing well and you are not able to do the same, it hurts a bit.

Stenshorne has also set out his goals for the rest of the season

“But I knew what I was capable of, and I feel like so far this year, we've shown what we can do, even though the results have not always been the best. But if you look a bit behind the results and see our pace, I think we were very good.”

GOAL FOR THE REST OF THE SEASON

Stenshorne also gave a little insight into his career goal, with his eyes, like most of the grid, set on Formula 1.

The 20-year-old feels to get to that level results have to be good, and while he acknowledges that his have not been the best recently, he says “even though the results haven’t always been there, I hope that they still see that the pace has been there. So I hope that's enough.”

READ MORE

Dino Beganovic on the 2026 season, learning from Hamilton and Leclerc and gaining confidence with Ferrari

Formula 2 in 2020: Crazy races, memorable victories and a couple of F1 graduates

Stenshorne is still keen to get his results back to where they were at the start of the year following the summer break.

“For sure the goal is just to win races like we did in the beginning of the year,” he concludes. “I want to fight for podiums more regularly, also in the Feature Races, so for sure that's the goal now.

“Hopefully we finish well in the championship, that's of course also the goal, but short term focus is on each race and just trying to end the season on a high.”
